newsitem.title: USA: Rosanne finds work as talk show host.
newsitem.headline: Rosanne finds work as talk show host.

text.p: Move over Oprah. Watch out Rosie. Roseanne has a new job in your chosen field.
Just hours before her nine-year-long situation comedy aired its last episode Tuesday night on ABC, Roseanne announced that she had found a new job as a talk show host.
And at a love-in at the posh 21 Club with her new bosses, Michael and Roger King of King World Productions Inc., the comedian announced that she doesn't have to show up for work until 1998.
Roseanne had to carefully squeeze that in between the praise heaped on her by the King brothers, who duelled with each other to see who could sing her praises loudest and longest.
"Roseanne is the brightest star in the history of television to go from prime time to daytime TV," Michael King declared as Roger King added, "She will take the talk show into a new era."
Roseanne's manager, Jeff Wald, then chimed in, "Every studio and company in Hollywood appealed to us to do a talk show. They threw money at our feet. But King World is the best."

Michael King then added, "Look at what Roseanne did for ABC. That show generated several billion dollars. We are stroking Roseanne's ego (for good reason). TV needs a star of this magnitude coming into daytime."
Both King brothers stressed that Roseanne's new show will not compete with Oprah Winfrey or the Rosie O'Donnell programmes but will be syndicated at different times.

They disclosed few details of the deal but said that Roseanne will be given stock in King World. Winfrey, whose programme is distributed by King World, is already a stockholder and the Kings said she was delighted at having Roseanne on board.
They also disclosed few details about the show. Roseanne said the show did not have a name yet or a production staff and the only thing she knew was that she wanted Oprah and Rosie on as guests.
The programme will be on daytime television for an hour a day, five days a week.

"I haven't had a show that's generated this much reaction since 'Oprah.'" Roger King said. "Stations are coming at us already, and we believe that this will be among the biggest debuts in syndicated television history."
